--- title: "Repeated Measures ANOVA" subtitle: "PSYC 6019-A01 / PSYC 6022-A01
2026-11-06 | Lab 11" author: "Jess Helmer" footer: "[jhelmer3.github.io/PSYC6019-2026](https://jhelmer3.github.io/PSYC6019-2026/)" format: revealjs: code-link: true slide-number: true code-line-numbers: false theme: ../../gt-theme.scss width: 1200 execute: echo: true dpi: 600 freeze: auto knitr: opts_chunk: dev: svg --- ## Outline - Repeated measures ANOVA - Mixed effect ANOVA - Multilevel modeling ::: {.cell} ::: # Repeated Measures ANOVA ## Repeated Measures ANOVA It is sometimes the case that we have *repeated measures* data ::: subpoint ○ Responses collected on the same measure for the same subjects more than one time ::: Some examples of repeated measures data are... ::: subpoint ○ A mental health screening questionnaire given to participants once per day ::: ::: subpoint ○ A yearly customer satisfaction survey ::: For these designs, we have to consider if conditions are **between-person** or **within-person**. ## Repeated Measures Model ## Repeated Measures Example :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="85%"} Remember the chick dataset from Lab 06? We are going to use... another chick dataset! Instead of having one value of chick weight for each chick, this one tracks chicks over time. We will have weekly updates on each chick's weight. ::: ::: {.column width="15%"} ![](https://mannapro.com/cdn/shop/articles/how-to-raise-baby-chickens_2x_b6a71ebc-2d08-4bdc-82b0-18ccf861c9bd.jpg?v=1740003489) ::: :::: ## Repeated Measures Example ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chick_data <- read_csv(here::here("lab", "data", "lab_11", "chick_week_data.csv")) chick_data ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 180 × 4 chick diet week weight 1 13 1 0 60 2 13 1 1 71 3 13 1 2 91 4 13 1 3 96 5 9 1 0 68 6 9 1 1 90 7 9 1 2 100 8 9 1 3 98 9 20 1 0 58 10 20 1 1 77 # ℹ 170 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## Repeated Measures Example ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # install.packages("psych") psych::describe(chick_data) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` vars n mean sd median trimmed mad min max range skew kurtosis chick 1 180 26.09 14.56 27.0 26.24 19.27 1 50 49 -0.11 -1.18 diet 2 180 2.27 1.15 2.0 2.21 1.48 1 4 3 0.27 -1.39 week 3 180 1.50 1.12 1.5 1.50 1.48 0 3 3 0.00 -1.38 weight 4 180 159.48 78.37 147.5 151.85 92.66 58 373 315 0.64 -0.55 se chick 1.09 diet 0.09 week 0.08 weight 5.84 ``` ::: ::: ## Repeated Measures Example We want to estimate the effect of week of the experiment on chick weight! Is `week` a between- or within-subject (chick) factor? [Within!]{.fragment} [What about diet?]{.fragment} [Between!]{.fragment} ::: fragment Can see in the data that within every chick (`.by = chick`), there are four levels of week (`n_distinct(week)`) but only one level of diet (`n_distinct(diet)`). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chick_data |> summarize( .by = chick, n_diets = n_distinct(diet), n_weeks = n_distinct(week) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 45 × 3 chick n_diets n_weeks 1 13 1 4 2 9 1 4 3 20 1 4 4 10 1 4 5 17 1 4 6 19 1 4 7 4 1 4 8 6 1 4 9 11 1 4 10 3 1 4 # ℹ 35 more rows ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Repeated Measures Example ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chick_data |> head(4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 4 chick diet week weight 1 13 1 0 60 2 13 1 1 71 3 13 1 2 91 4 13 1 3 96 ``` ::: ::: Notice that all the variables in this dataset are `double`s (decimal point numbers). The ANOVA functions want to treat these as `factor`s. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column .fragment width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chick_cleaned <- chick_data |> mutate(chick = factor(chick), week = factor(week), diet = factor(diet)) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column .fragment width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chick_cleaned <- chick_data |> mutate( across(c(chick, week, diet), factor) ) ``` ::: ::: :::: ## Aside: `across()` `across()` is a helpful `{tidyverse}` function that can be used within functions like `summarize()` and `mutate()`. When we want to apply the same transformation to multiple columns, we can target them all with `across()` and specify the transformation once, instead of manually specifying each one. `across(columns, function(s))` ::: subpoint ○ `columns` = `` columns to target ::: ::: subpoint ○ `function(s)` = name of function to use, *anonymous function*, or list of functions. ::: ## Aside: `across()` Examples of `across()`... ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Name of Function Just like we did before ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chick_data |> mutate(across(c(chick, week, diet), factor)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 180 × 4 chick diet week weight 1 13 1 0 60 2 13 1 1 71 3 13 1 2 91 4 13 1 3 96 5 9 1 0 68 6 9 1 1 90 7 9 1 2 100 8 9 1 3 98 9 20 1 0 58 10 20 1 1 77 # ℹ 170 more rows ``` ::: ::: ### Anonymous Function ::: {style="font-size:90%"} Example of standardizing across all columns (not necessarily helpful here). Reminder: within `function()`, `column` just serves as a placeholder name for that column. You can name this whatever you want, as long as you use the same name within the actual function part. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chick_data |> mutate(across(everything(), function(column) (column - mean(column)) / sd(column))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 180 × 4 chick diet week weight 1 -0.899 -1.11 -1.34 -1.27 2 -0.899 -1.11 -0.446 -1.13 3 -0.899 -1.11 0.446 -0.874 4 -0.899 -1.11 1.34 -0.810 5 -1.17 -1.11 -1.34 -1.17 6 -1.17 -1.11 -0.446 -0.887 7 -1.17 -1.11 0.446 -0.759 8 -1.17 -1.11 1.34 -0.784 9 -0.418 -1.11 -1.34 -1.29 10 -0.418 -1.11 -0.446 -1.05 # ℹ 170 more rows ``` ::: ::: ### List of Functions Example of summarizing columns by multiple functions ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chick_data |> summarize(across( where(is.numeric), list(min = min, max = max, mean = function(column) mean(column, na.rm = T)) )) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 12 chick_min chick_max chick_mean diet_min diet_max diet_mean week_min week_max 1 1 50 26.1 1 4 2.27 0 3 # ℹ 4 more variables: week_mean , weight_min , weight_max , # weight_mean ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Aside: `across()` Our original `across()` method successfully converted the intended columns to `factor()`s. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chick_cleaned <- chick_data |> mutate( across(c(chick, week, diet), factor) ) chick_cleaned ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 180 × 4 chick diet week weight 1 13 1 0 60 2 13 1 1 71 3 13 1 2 91 4 13 1 3 96 5 9 1 0 68 6 9 1 1 90 7 9 1 2 100 8 9 1 3 98 9 20 1 0 58 10 20 1 1 77 # ℹ 170 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## Repeated Measures Example `ez::ezANOVA(data, dv, wid, within = NULL, between = NULL, type = 2)` ::: subpoint ○ `dv` = the outcome variable ::: ::: subpoint ○ `wid` = name of the column with subject identifier. Typically contains an `id` for each person (here, each chick!) ::: ::: subpoint ○ `within` = column(s) with within-subject factors ::: ::: subpoint ○ `between` = column(s) with between-subject factors ::: ::: subpoint ○ `type` = the sums of squares method used ::: `= NULL` means the default is set to `NULL`, and you do not necessarily need to input a value for that argument for the function to work. (May need to specify it for the function to work the way you *want*, though! Depends on your ANOVA goal.) ## Balanced or Unbalanced :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chick_cleaned |> count(week) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 2 week n 1 0 45 2 1 45 3 2 45 4 3 45 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} What type of Sums of Squares should we use? [Doesn't matter!]{.fragment} ::: :::: ## Repeated Measures Example `ez::ezANOVA(data, dv, wid, within = NULL, between = NULL, type = 2)` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chick_weight_model <- ez::ezANOVA( data = chick_cleaned, dv = weight, wid = chick, within = week ) chick_weight_model ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $ANOVA Effect DFn DFd F p p<.05 ges 2 week 3 132 184.9641 4.388747e-47 * 0.5768658 $`Mauchly's Test for Sphericity` Effect W p p<.05 2 week 0.006591028 2.933872e-44 * $`Sphericity Corrections` Effect GGe p[GG] p[GG]<.05 HFe p[HF] p[HF]<.05 2 week 0.375836 2.894679e-19 * 0.3789365 2.103585e-19 * ``` ::: ::: ## Assumptions ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chick_cleaned |> pivot_wider(names_from = week, names_prefix = "week_", values_from = weight) |> select(starts_with("week")) |> cov() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` week_0 week_1 week_2 week_3 week_0 70.16364 215.8788 313.9909 318.0485 week_1 215.87879 1031.9495 1702.1818 1756.9066 week_2 313.99091 1702.1818 4357.6091 4694.9864 week_3 318.04848 1756.9066 4694.9864 5113.7192 ``` ::: ::: **Sphericity**: are the elements on the diagonal all equal in the population? **Compound Symmetry**: are the elements on the diagonal AND on the off-diagonals all equal in the population? ## Assumptions If assumption holds, `W` should be close to 1 and `p` will be large ($p > .05$). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chick_weight_model$`Mauchly's Test for Sphericity` ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Effect W p p<.05 2 week 0.006591028 2.933872e-44 * ``` ::: ::: ## Assumptions Corrections ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chick_weight_model$`Sphericity Corrections` ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Effect GGe p[GG] p[GG]<.05 HFe p[HF] p[HF]<.05 2 week 0.375836 2.894679e-19 * 0.3789365 2.103585e-19 * ``` ::: ::: ## Results ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chick_weight_model ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $ANOVA Effect DFn DFd F p p<.05 ges 2 week 3 132 184.9641 4.388747e-47 * 0.5768658 $`Mauchly's Test for Sphericity` Effect W p p<.05 2 week 0.006591028 2.933872e-44 * $`Sphericity Corrections` Effect GGe p[GG] p[GG]<.05 HFe p[HF] p[HF]<.05 2 week 0.375836 2.894679e-19 * 0.3789365 2.103585e-19 * ``` ::: ::: We observe a significant effect of week on chick weight. ## Estimated Marginal Means ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} emmeans::emmeans(chick_weight_model) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error: ! Can't handle an object of class "list" Use help("models", package = "emmeans") for information on supported models. ``` ::: ::: `ezANOVA()` returns dataframes, and `emmeans()` isn't able to turn those into EMMS. You'd have to refit with `return_aov = T` and also make sure the contrasts have been set to orthogonal before (even if it is a balanced design!). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} options(contrasts = c("contr.sum", "contr.poly")) chick_weight_model <- ez::ezANOVA( data = chick_cleaned, dv = weight, wid = chick, within = week, return_aov = T ) chick_weight_model$aov |> emmeans::emmeans("week") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` week emmean SE df lower.CL upper.CL 0 74.9 7.66 89.5 59.6 90.1 1 132.8 7.66 89.5 117.6 148.0 2 211.6 7.66 89.5 196.4 226.8 3 218.7 7.66 89.5 203.5 233.9 Warning: EMMs are biased unless design is perfectly balanced Confidence level used: 0.95 ``` ::: ::: That's an annoying extra step to deal with... ## Resetting ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} options(contrasts = c("contr.treatment", "contr.poly")) ``` ::: ## `afex` ANOVAs Unfortunately, the `{ez}` package is not being maintained very much right now, so it is less equipped to integrate with other tools like `{emmeans}`. Another package with ANOVA functionality, `{afex}`, is! It has many ways of specifying the form of the ANOVA you want to estimate, including one very similar to the `ezANOVA()` syntax. `afex::aov_ez(id, dv, data, between = NULL, within = NULL, type = 3)` ::: subpoint ○ `id` = **character vector** name of the column with subject identifier ::: ::: subpoint ○ `dv` = **character vector** the outcome variable ::: ::: subpoint ○ `within` = **character vector** column(s) with within-subject factors ::: ::: subpoint ○ `between` = **character vector** column(s) with between-subject factors ::: ::: subpoint ○ `type` = the sums of squares method used ::: Note that `afex::aov_ez()` uses Type III sums of squares by default. ## `afex` ANOVAs Unfortunately, the `{ez}` package is not being maintained very much right now, so it is less equipped to integrate with other tools like `{emmeans}`. Another package with ANOVA functionality, `{afex}`, is! It has many ways of specifying the form of the ANOVA you want to estimate, including one very similar to the `ezANOVA()` syntax. `afex::aov_ez(id, dv, data, between = NULL, within = NULL, type = 3)` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chick_weight_model_afex <- afex::aov_ez( data = chick_cleaned, dv = "weight", id = "chick", within = "week" ) summary(chick_weight_model_afex) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Univariate Type III Repeated-Measures ANOVA Assuming Sphericity Sum Sq num Df Error SS den Df F value Pr(>F) (Intercept) 4578288 1 314352 44 640.83 < 2.2e-16 *** week 634258 3 150880 132 184.96 < 2.2e-16 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Mauchly Tests for Sphericity Test statistic p-value week 0.006591 2.9339e-44 Greenhouse-Geisser and Huynh-Feldt Corrections for Departure from Sphericity GG eps Pr(>F[GG]) week 0.37584 < 2.2e-16 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 HF eps Pr(>F[HF]) week 0.3789365 2.103585e-19 ``` ::: ::: ## Estimated Marginal Means ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} emms_week <- emmeans::emmeans(chick_weight_model_afex, specs = "week") emms_week ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` week emmean SE df lower.CL upper.CL X0 74.9 1.25 44 72.4 77.4 X1 132.8 4.79 44 123.1 142.4 X2 211.6 9.84 44 191.8 231.4 X3 218.7 10.70 44 197.2 240.2 Confidence level used: 0.95 ``` ::: ::: Note than `emmeans()` slightly adjusted the labeling of the week value. We can prevent that by going back to data cleaning and not letting the levels within that variable start with a number. ## Estimated Marginal Means :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chick_cleaned <- chick_data |> mutate( across(c(chick, week, diet), factor), week = paste0("week_", week) ) chick_cleaned ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 180 × 4 chick diet week weight 1 13 1 week_0 60 2 13 1 week_1 71 3 13 1 week_2 91 4 13 1 week_3 96 5 9 1 week_0 68 6 9 1 week_1 90 7 9 1 week_2 100 8 9 1 week_3 98 9 20 1 week_0 58 10 20 1 week_1 77 # ℹ 170 more rows ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chick_weight_model_afex <- afex::aov_ez( data = chick_cleaned, dv = "weight", id = "chick", within = "week" ) emms_week <- emmeans::emmeans(chick_weight_model_afex, specs = "week") emms_week ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` week emmean SE df lower.CL upper.CL week_0 74.9 1.25 44 72.4 77.4 week_1 132.8 4.79 44 123.1 142.4 week_2 211.6 9.84 44 191.8 231.4 week_3 218.7 10.70 44 197.2 240.2 Confidence level used: 0.95 ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Visualization ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Plot ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_11_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-24-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: ### Code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # install.packages("ggdist") emms_week |> as_tibble() |> ggplot(aes(x = week, y = emmean, ymin = lower.CL, ymax = upper.CL)) + ggdist::geom_dots( data = chick_cleaned, aes(x = week, y = weight), inherit.aes = F, alpha = 0.4) + geom_point() + geom_linerange() + scale_x_discrete(labels = parse_number) + # applying the `parse_number()` function to the labels labs(y = "Weight", x = "Week", caption = "Line ranges represent 95% confidence intervals. Gray points represent observed data.") + guides(x = guide_axis(cap = T), y = guide_axis(cap = T)) + theme_classic() ``` ::: ::: # Mixed ANOVA ## Mixed ANOVA We aren't just limited to between- **OR** within-subject factors, can also test combinations of both. ## Mixed ANOVA Example We can also consider the effect of diet given to the chicks on their weight! ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chick_weight_diet_model <- afex::aov_ez( data = chick_cleaned, dv = "weight", id = "chick", within = "week", between = "diet" ) summary(chick_weight_diet_model) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Univariate Type III Repeated-Measures ANOVA Assuming Sphericity Sum Sq num Df Error SS den Df F value Pr(>F) (Intercept) 4599758 1 226112 41 834.0544 < 2.2e-16 *** diet 88239 3 226112 41 5.3333 0.0033949 ** week 649354 3 118752 123 224.1940 < 2.2e-16 *** diet:week 32127 9 118752 123 3.6974 0.0003951 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Mauchly Tests for Sphericity Test statistic p-value week 0.009022 2.213e-38 diet:week 0.009022 2.213e-38 Greenhouse-Geisser and Huynh-Feldt Corrections for Departure from Sphericity GG eps Pr(>F[GG]) week 0.38347 < 2e-16 *** diet:week 0.38347 0.01413 * --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 HF eps Pr(>F[HF]) week 0.387433 8.827052e-21 diet:week 0.387433 1.379698e-02 ``` ::: ::: ## Balanced or Unbalanced :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chick_cleaned |> count(week, diet) |> pivot_wider(names_from = diet, names_prefix = "week_", values_from = n) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 5 week week_1 week_2 week_3 week_4 1 week_0 16 10 10 9 2 week_1 16 10 10 9 3 week_2 16 10 10 9 4 week_3 16 10 10 9 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} What type of Sums of Squares should we use? [Do we think an interaction between week and diet would be negligible?]{.fragment} [Maybe not! Let's do Type III]{.fragment} [`afex` does Type III sums of squares by default... and also automatically changes the contrasts to `contr.sum`!]{.fragment} ::: :::: ## Mixed ANOVA Example We can also consider the effect of diet given to the chicks on their weight! ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} options(contrasts = c("contr.sum", "contr.poly")) chick_weight_diet_model_ez <- ez::ezANOVA( data = chick_cleaned, dv = weight, wid = chick, within = week, between = diet, type = 3 ) chick_weight_diet_model ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Anova Table (Type 3 tests) Response: weight Effect df MSE F ges p.value 1 diet 3, 41 5514.94 5.33 ** .204 .003 2 week 1.15, 47.17 2517.71 224.19 *** .653 <.001 3 diet:week 3.45, 47.17 2517.71 3.70 * .085 .014 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '+' 0.1 ' ' 1 Sphericity correction method: GG ``` ::: ::: ## Visualization ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} emms_week_diet <- emmeans::emmeans(chick_weight_diet_model, specs = c("diet", "week")) emms_week_diet ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` diet week emmean SE df lower.CL upper.CL 1 week_0 67.7 1.50 41 64.7 70.7 2 week_0 75.4 1.89 41 71.6 79.2 3 week_0 77.9 1.89 41 74.1 81.7 4 week_0 83.7 2.00 41 79.6 87.7 1 week_1 114.4 7.26 41 99.8 129.1 2 week_1 131.3 9.18 41 112.8 149.8 3 week_1 144.4 9.18 41 125.9 162.9 4 week_1 154.1 9.68 41 134.6 173.7 1 week_2 173.2 14.70 41 143.6 202.9 2 week_2 205.6 18.50 41 168.1 243.1 3 week_2 258.9 18.50 41 221.4 296.4 4 week_2 233.9 19.50 41 194.4 273.4 1 week_3 177.8 16.00 41 145.4 210.1 2 week_3 214.7 20.20 41 173.8 255.6 3 week_3 270.3 20.20 41 229.4 311.2 4 week_3 238.6 21.30 41 195.5 281.6 Confidence level used: 0.95 ``` ::: ::: ## Light points represent observed data.") + guides(x = guide_axis(cap = T), y = guide_axis(cap = T)) + theme_classic() ``` ::: ::: ## Visualization ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Plot ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_11_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-32-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: ### Code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} emms_week_diet |> as_tibble() |> ggplot(aes(x = week, y = emmean, ymin = lower.CL, ymax = upper.CL, color = diet, group = diet)) + ggdist::geom_dots( data = chick_cleaned, aes(x = week, y = weight, color = diet), inherit.aes = F, alpha = 0.4, position = position_dodge(.5)) + geom_point(position = position_dodge(.5)) + geom_linerange(position = position_dodge(.5)) + geom_line(position = position_dodge(.5)) + scale_x_discrete(labels = parse_number) + # applying the `parse_number()` function to the labels labs(y = "Weight", x = "Week", color = "Diet", caption = "Line ranges represent 95% confidence intervals. Light points represent observed data.") + guides(x = guide_axis(cap = T), y = guide_axis(cap = T), color = guide_none()) + facet_wrap("diet", labeller = "label_both") + theme_classic() ``` ::: ::: # Multilevel Modeling ## Multilevel Modeling Multilevel Modeling (MLM) is a more flexible framework for examining between- and within-subject variation! ANOVA can't handle missing cells (e.g., if we were missing weight observations for diet 3 in week 4), but MLM can! <script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
